content:
Quick answer: Osteoarthritis in both knees does not automatically qualify you for PIP, and it does not rule you out. Eligibility depends on the specific daily living and mobility activities you can do reliably, alongside age, residence and other rules. Explain your own walking and everyday difficulties, help or aids you need, and how your ability varies. Do not copy another person's distances or describe every day as your worst day.

Start with eligibility, not the number of affected knees

GOV.UK's PIP eligibility guidance says you must be 16 or over, have a long-term condition or disability, have difficulty with certain everyday tasks or getting around, and expect those difficulties to last at least 12 months from when they started. You usually need to be under State Pension age to make a new claim. Exceptions and residence rules apply. Working or having savings does not itself prevent PIP.

For England and Wales use the official PIP claim route. Northern Ireland has its own PIP claim service. In Scotland, check Adult Disability Payment rather than assuming a new DWP PIP claim is the right route. Our PIP eligibility guide explains the broader questions.

Explain what you can do reliably

The DWP assessment criteria require activities to be considered safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and within a reasonable time. For this test, reasonable time means no more than twice the maximum time a person without the relevant impairment would normally take. Being able to attempt something once is not the whole assessment.

Describe better and worse days and how often each occurs. Explain when pain, stiffness or fatigue affects an activity and what happens afterwards. The assessment guide includes rules for fluctuating conditions over a 12-month period; a single unusually bad day does not describe that whole period.

Daily living: use examples tied to a named activity

Daily living and mobility are assessed separately. Relevant daily living activities may include preparing food, washing and bathing, dressing, and managing treatment. Do not assume that a difficulty with a household task automatically corresponds to a particular PIP descriptor.

  • Preparing food: explain what happens when you prepare and cook a simple meal, whether you need to sit or use an aid, and whether another person is needed. Give the frequency and what happens without that support.
  • Washing and bathing: describe getting into or out of the bath or shower, any necessary aid or physical help, and a specific safety difficulty if there is one.
  • Dressing: describe socks, shoes or lower-body clothing if knee movement affects them. Say what help is needed and how long the activity takes, rather than only saying that bending hurts.
  • Managing treatment: describe a genuine difficulty with the treatment activity if it applies. Do not assume knee osteoarthritis must affect opening medicine bottles or that taking medicine automatically scores points.

These are prompts for accurate evidence, not qualifying thresholds or instructions to claim difficulties you do not have. Explain other relevant conditions too: the decision concerns your needs, not whether every difficulty can be attributed to one diagnosis.

Walking and getting around: keep the two mobility activities distinct

The DWP guide separates moving around from planning and following journeys. Moving around considers standing and physical movement. Planning and following journeys concerns limitations arising from mental health, cognitive or sensory impairments. Physical difficulty climbing transport steps or walking across a car park is not, by itself, evidence of difficulty planning or following a route.

For physical walking difficulty, describe a realistic distance, the surface and aid used, why you stop, how long you need to rest and whether you could repeat the distance when reasonably required. Do not force your answer into a distance you have seen on a website. Avoid unsafe walking tests just to collect evidence. Use distances and examples you can explain honestly, with any uncertainty made clear.

Illustrative evidence structure: “On this route I could move approximately this far, using this aid. I stopped because of this difficulty, rested for this long, and could or could not repeat it later. This happens on this many days.” Fill it with your own experience, including when you can manage further.

What NICE and NHS guidance can and cannot establish

The NHS osteoarthritis overview explains that symptoms vary greatly and can affect everyday activities. NICE NG226, recommendations 1.1.2 and 1.2.2, says imaging is not routinely needed to diagnose osteoarthritis and care should be guided by symptoms and physical function. These are clinical recommendations, not PIP entitlement rules. Do not arrange an X-ray solely because you assume one is required for PIP. Describe your actual support needs and use the DWP assessment criteria for benefit activities.

Gather useful information without delaying the form

GOV.UK suggests supporting documents such as prescription lists, care plans and information from your doctor or others involved in your care. Existing physiotherapy or occupational therapy reports may help describe function. A diagnosis or X-ray alone does not explain every activity, and no particular report guarantees an award.

Keep a short diary of specific activities and the help you need, including better days. Do not wait to complete a preferred diary period if a form deadline is approaching. The official claim guidance says to complete the disability form within one month and to contact the PIP enquiry line if you need more time. Keep copies and follow the deadline and contact details sent with your own form.

If you disagree with a decision

For England and Wales, you can usually ask for mandatory reconsideration within one month of the date on your decision letter, by phone, letter or the official form. If writing, it must arrive by then. Explain the disputed activities and reasons. If you are late, contact the office promptly and explain why; acceptance is not automatic.

If you still disagree after reconsideration, an appeal to the independent tribunal is free and normally due within one month of getting the reconsideration decision. Check the different routes for Northern Ireland and Social Security Scotland decisions. Our PIP appeal guide explains the sequence. Do not assume a fresh claim replaces an appeal or protects its deadline. Citizens Advice warns that challenging the amount or length of an existing award can lead to the whole claim being looked at again, so payments could be reduced or stopped. Get advice about that risk.

Get individual help where needed

Citizens Advice explains how decisions and points work. A welfare-rights adviser can help you understand the descriptors, evidence and options. Ask what support is available locally rather than assuming representation is guaranteed.

Next step: check your official claim route, write down the activities affected and collect concrete examples.
